item.title: What vaccines doctors say you may need for respiratory virus season
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As the weather turns colder, it also means respiratory virus season is upon the United States. In its annual outlook report , the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it expects the 2026-27 respiratory virus season to have a similar number of peak hospitalizations from influenza, COVID-19 and RSV compared to last season. Public health specialists told ABC News the best way for people to protect themselves against these viruses is to get vaccinated. Expert tips for parents to prepare as flu season begins Flu vaccine The CDC currently recommends that people aged 6 months and older receive an annual flu vaccine. The seasonal flu vaccine protects against three viruses predicted to circulate during flu season: Type A (H1N1) virus, Type A(H3N2) virus, and Type B/Victoria virus. There are several flu vaccines available this season, with recommendations varying by age and medical history. Mary Conlon/AP Photo - PHOTO: A box of flu vaccines is displayed at a pharmacy in New York, Sept. 15, 2026. "Obviously, we target high-risk groups, so those would be older adults, so over the age of 50, people with chronic medical conditions, individuals who are immunocompromised, individuals that have obesity, or persons who are pregnant or wanting to get pregnant, and healthcare personnel," Dr. Michael Angarone, director of the Infectious Disease Fellowship Program at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, told ABC News. "But I recommend every patient that I see should get vaccinated for influenza." Standard-dose inactivated flu vaccines grown either in eggs or cell culture are available for anybody as young as 6 months old. High-dose and adjuvanted flu vaccines, both of which are egg-based, are available for those aged 65 and older due to their higher risk of severe illness. Anyone aged 9 and older can receive a recombinant flu vaccine, which is produced without eggs. For those between ages 2 and 49, who don't have certain medical conditions and aren't pregnant, a nasal spray flu vaccine is also available. Additionally, in August, the Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine to protect those aged 50 and older. New York declares state disaster emergency over rising measles cases. Here's what that means One dose is recommended for children between 6 months and 8 years old who have received two doses in past seasons and everyone aged 9 and older. Some children under age 9 may require two doses based on prior vaccine history. Public health specialists told ABC News they recommend that people receive flu vaccines by the end of October, but that people should get the vaccine even if later in the fall or winter as long as influenza viruses are circulating and unexpired vaccine is available. Dr. Majd Alsoubani, infectious disease physician at Tufts Medical Center, said that one thing she often hears from patients is that every time they receive the vaccine, they get the flu -- which she says is a combination of misinformation and misunderstanding. "All the injectable influenza vaccines, they don't have the live virus, it only contains parts of the virus, so it doesn't cause influenza," she told ABC News. "We know that the vaccine needs a couple of weeks just to create protection, so if they were exposed to influenza before the vaccine or right after, they actually might get the flu because the vaccine didn't have time to provide that protection." COVID-19 vaccine People aged 18 and older are recommended to receive the COVID-19 vaccine, as are children ages 6 months to 17 years old at increased risk. Parents of all other children should speak to their pediatrician to discuss getting the vaccine. The updated 2026-2027 COVID-19 vaccines target the XFG strain, a recombinant Omicron variant, meaning it formed through the combination of two Omicron subvariants. Moderna's mRNA vaccine is approved for those 6 months through 64 years old with an underlying condition and for all adults aged 65 and older. Another Moderna mRNA vaccine that is a lower dosage is available for those ages 12 and older. Pfizer's mRNA vaccine is approved for those 5 years through 64 years old with an underlying condition and for all adults over age 65. Mary Conlon/AP Photo - PHOTO: A box of COVID-19 mRNA vaccines is displayed at a pharmacy in New York, Sept. 15, 2026. According to the CDC, underlying conditions placing people at risk for higher risk for severe COVID-19 include but are not limited to cancer, asthma, chronic lung disease, diabetes, heart conditions, mental health conditions and pregnancy. Also available is a vaccine from Novavax, which is a protein-based vaccine, for those aged 12 and older. Angarone said people can safely get the flu and COVID vaccine during the same visit if they are eligible. "I recommend to my patients just get it at the same time, or if you don't want to get both at the same time, get [the COVID vaccine] a week apart from the flu vaccine," he said. "So, kind of around this time, October timeframe." When to get a flu shot: See what new option is available RSV vaccine "The immunization recommendation kind of follows the people who are at risk of severe disease," Alsoubani said. "So the RSV vaccine currently is only one dose, so you're one and done. It's not an annual vaccine." The CDC recommends RSV vaccines for all adults aged 75 and older and adults between ages 50 and 74 at increased risk for severe RSV. It is also recommended for all pregnant people between 32 and 36 weeks' gestation. Mary Conlon/AP - PHOTO: A box of RSV vaccine is displayed at a pharmacy in New York, Sept. 24, 2024. For infants under 8 months who are in their first RSV season and whose mother did not receive a maternal RSV vaccine, two monoclonal antibody shots are available. Monoclonal antibodies are proteins manufactured in a lab that mimic the antibodies the body naturally creates when fighting an infection. A small group of young children between ages 8-19 months at increased risk for severe RSV may also be eligible. item.title: GOP efforts to lower gas prices derailed by Republican infighting
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republican efforts to reduce national gas prices in the weeks before Election Day were derailed in the Senate by infighting among GOP lawmakers and members of the administration who could not agree on how to ease consumers’ pain at the pump. The divisions within the Senate Republican conference over how to lower gas and diesel prices — even if temporarily — were driven primarily by geographic differences. Senators from oil-refining states shot down proposals from farm-state senators to ban the export of diesel or to loosen restrictions on the sale of E15 gasoline with higher ethanol content. “You’re talking about regional politics, and it gets bogged down in the politics of energy, and the fiefdoms around it,” said Ron Bonjean, a GOP strategist and former Senate leadership aide. There were divisions that went beyond geography, too. Fiscal hawks torpedoed proposals to suspend the gas tax, even though their colleagues argued that doing so for a short period of time to bolster Republican candidates would have little real impact on the highway trust fund. And lawmakers had less flexibility on some possible actions because of the depletion of the nation’s strategic petroleum reserve by big drawdowns to stabilize market prices during the Iran war. The biggest problem, however, was that Republican senators didn’t see any proposal as likely to have a significant impact on prices before Nov. 3, when voters will decide which party controls Congress next year. “It is almost impossible to federally reduce gasoline prices for consumers because the levers of power that can be used have very little effect on the prices,” Bonjean said. The idea that appeared to have the most momentum was a proposal to impose a 90-day ban on diesel exports, which Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) began floating before a Senate Republican leadership meeting in mid-September. “We need to concentrate on affordability for this election. With diesel at $6, the best thing [President] Trump could do is follow what a Republican president did in the '70s and a Democrat president did in the '70s — when they were worried about the price of food, they put an embargo on soybeans and wheat — and [Trump] should put an embargo on diesel leaving the country,” Grassley told The Hill on Sept. 14. Trump embraced the idea, but it immediately ran into heavy resistance from oil-state senators and oil companies, who argued that it wouldn’t cut diesel prices but instead might even push them higher. “One thing we know for sure is that export bans don’t have a negative price impact, particularly with a commodity like that that’s globally traded and globally priced,” said Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.). “If you restrict access to the global market for our diesel production, you literally disincentivize more diesel production in which case you end up with higher prices, lower supply,” he said. “You’re restricting your global supply, which has a global impact on prices.” Cramer warned that a diesel export ban “most likely would” raise diesel prices, especially in California and the Northeast, which import diesel from foreign sources. Sen. John Cornyn (R), who represents oil-rich Texas, dismissed the proposed diesel export ban as a “gimmick.” The White House in late September floated a plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days, despite objections from Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who argued that “banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work.” Trump ruled out the idea last week before heading to Ohio to campaign for embattled Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio). Earlier this year, fiscal hawks such as Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) spoke out against a proposal introduced by Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) to suspend the gas tax. The federal gas tax is 18.4 cents a gallon for gasoline and 24.4 cents a gallon for diesel. Hawley argued it would give American workers and families “immediate relief,” but Paul and other budget hawks warned it would blow a hole in the highway trust fund. Another proposal floated by farm-state Republican senators alarmed by the voter backlash to high gas prices was to allow permanent easing of restrictions on E15 gasoline, a fuel blend that includes 15 percent ethanol. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), who’s up for reelection this year, touted E15 as a way to knock down fuel prices. “It would bring it down right now, some people think, as much as 30 cents a gallon — do voluntary E15 nationwide. It would be immediately available. It’s there now. It’s an American product,” Rounds told The Hill. “The president could do that today,” he said. Rounds also called for expanding refining capacity in the United States. But Republicans from oil-producing states argued that wider availability of E15 gas would hurt small- and mid-size oil refiners. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) declared his opposition to what he called the “year-round E15 mandate” after Lee Zeldin, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), announced in March that the Trump administration would expand the sales of gasoline with higher concentrations of ethanol over the summer. The fight will continue to play out during the lame-duck session of Congress after the Nov. 3 elections. Campaigning with Senate Republican candidate Michele Tafoya in Minnesota this week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said he was optimistic about passing legislation to boost the availability of E15 gas in the stalled farm bill. “I intend and expect fully to get this done and get it across the finish line,” Thune said of the farm bill. “And it will include E15, exact version maybe to be determined.” Thune’s comments were reported by local radio station WZFG's “The Flag.” Even so, GOP strategists are doubtful that Washington can do much to impact the price of gas unless Trump finds a military or diplomatic solution to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has used to choke off much of the global oil supply. “It’s very hard to predict where gas prices are going to be after the election but one could put money down it’s still going to be high,” said Bonjean, the GOP strategist. He said, however, that prices could come down dramatically if Trump is able to eliminate Iranian threats to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz using serious “military intervention” — something the president has alluded to in recent days. item.title: From Abdul El-Sayed to James Talarico, 5 races and 5 keys to the midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON − In November, does the blue wave become a tsunami? Watch these spaces. Five keys are shaping monster midterms that are poised to revive Democrats' political power in Washington and reinforce it across the country. But the advantage of Republican money and the weakness of the Democratic Party brand could also mean an Election Night with more modest gains, a GOP catastrophe averted. In a wave election, Democrats regain control of the House of Representatives. In a tsunami, they take the Senate, too. The Texas Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico and a handful of tight Texas House races will show how many Hispanic voters are abandoning their brief alliance with the GOP. The Senate race in Michigan between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers will test whether swing-state voters are willing to support the Democrats' rising voices on the left. And President Donald Trump 's cross-country tour of some of the nation's most reliably Republican states, from Alabama to Oklahoma, will demonstrate whether he can still deliver. His voters have reshaped the GOP and twice elected him to the White House, but he's no longer on the ballot − not to mention that his approval ratings have sunk to the lowest level of any modern president as midterms approach. Even Kansas , which hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1932, has a too-close-to-call Senate contest. Here's how to track what's happening, and why. Do Hispanics come back? Watch: Texas Senate, Paxton v. Talarico Texas congressional districts 28, 34, 35 Trump was in San Antonio Oct. 7, his third trip to Texas in 30 days, courting Latino voters who had swung his way in 2024. "The Hispanics love me," he said fondly during a trip last year to the U.S.-Mexican border. Not so much now, though. Two years ago, Trump scored a breakthrough with Hispanics. In Texas, where they make up nearly a third of eligible voters, he carried them by 11 points after narrowly losing them in 2020. But they supported Talarico over Paxton by an overwhelming 63%-30% in a TelevisaUnivision/Cook Political Report poll taken Aug. 26-Sept. 3. Concern about inflation and alarm over the administration's aggressive efforts to deport illegal immigrants have eroded the GOP's standing. That has been one factor of several that have helped give Talarico a small but steady edge in statewide polls. Paxton has been a scandal-scarred attorney general who won the nomination only after a bitter primary battle against Sen. John Cornyn that divided the GOP. The changing loyalties of Hispanic voters have also thrown a wrench in Republican efforts to gain five Democratic-held House seats by redrawing their districts, a calculation that had counted in part on GOP gains among Hispanics. But Democratic incumbents Henry Cuellar (in the 28th district) and Vicente Gonzalez (in the 34th) are now favored to win, and a new Hispanic-majority district in San Antonio (the 35th) is a tossup. That is presumably one reason Trump was in San Antonio Wednesday to stump for votes. Will swing voters embrace the left? Watch: Michigan Senate, El-Sayed v. Rogers With trouble in Senate races from Maine to Texas, Republicans figure their best shot at flipping a Democratic-held seat is in Michigan. In the primary, Democrats narrowly nominated progressive Abdul El-Sayed over the party establishment's centrist choice, Rep. Haley Stevens. Now his campaign against former congressman Mike Rogers will test whether voters in a quintessential swing state − Michigan voted twice for Barack Obama, twice for Donald Trump − will embrace candidates from the left. "We are here to break the map," New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a leader of the democratic socialist movement, said of the Michigan race at an Oct. 5 fundraiser in New York. "Because if you can win, if Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere." That is probably political hyperbole, given the significant Arab and Muslim population in Michigan and the historic strength of the Democratic Party in the state, advantages that wouldn't be factors everywhere. If elected, El-Sayed would be the nation's first Muslim senator. But the toss-up race is still a test. And in a sign of how crucial both parties view it, both are deploying their biggest guns. Trump is heading to the Wolverine State to campaign this month, and Obama will headline a get-out-the-vote rally in Detroit on Oct. 24. That would be a week before Election Day. Can Republican money stem the flood? Watch: Florida governor, Donalds v. Jolly In the Florida governors' race, combined campaign spending on behalf of Republican Byron Donalds had totaled about $77 million by September. That was nine times more − nine times − than the overall spending on behalf of Democrat David Jolly , about $8.2 million. It's not clear whether Jolly, a former Republican congressman, can overcome such a yawning financial disadvantage. A new YouGov poll , released Oct. 6, had him nearly tied with Donalds, 47%-45%. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rankings in September moved the race from "likely Republican" to the more competitive "lean Republican," but not yet to the "toss-up" category. At a rally in Tampa, Jolly was asked what it would take to win. "I need the national Democratic Party to come into Florida and start spending money," he replied. Money doesn't buy votes, of course, but it does field get-out-the-vote operation and enable a candidate's partisans to flood the airwaves in the campaign's closing days. Among the official party campaign committees, the GOP has reported raising about double the amount the Democratic ones have, $1.3 billion v. $613 million. Then there's the Trump-affiliated MAGA Inc. It had nearly $416 million in the bank in September, available to spend. That's the most of any super PAC in history. "Republicans have the money, the candidates, and the message, and we're putting every dollar to work to defy history and expand this majority in November," Rep. Richard Hudson of North Carolina, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, boasted when the group reported record-breaking fundraising. Democratic nominees in some of the highest-profile Senate races have matched or even out-raised their Republican opponents. But in a half-dozen gubernatorial contests − including Georgia, Wisconsin and Texas as well as Florida − the Democrat is competitive in the polls but not when it comes to money in the bank. That has complicated Democratic hopes of breaking some GOP trifectas − that is, states where Republicans hold the governorship and control both state legislative chambers, leaving Democrats nearly powerless. Those targets include Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Texas and elsewhere. In Texas, Latino leaders pressured Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, chair of the Democratic Governors Association, to spend another $10 million on behalf of Gina Hinojosa, an unexpectedly strong challenger to incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott. In an interview with USA TODAY , Beshear described the Democrats' dilemma. "To give an extra dollar one place, it comes from another," he said. Can Trump turn out his voters? Watch: South Carolina Senate, Graham v. Andrews When his Senate pal Lindsay Graham died , Trump pushed for the appointment of the senator's sister, Darline Graham , to temporarily fill the seat and then helped her win the contested Republican nomination, defeating a five-term Republican congressman. The president gave Graham his "Complete and Total Endorsement" and said he had asked her to run for the seat "For the Good of our Nation." With the primary won, South Carolina is so overwhelmingly Republican that her victory in the general election would usually be considered a given. Not this year, as it is turning out. No other contest is such a personal test of Trump's clout. Her Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, trailed by a single point in recent surveys by Trafalgar and InsiderAdvantage. A Rasmussen poll gave her a narrow 4-point lead. In one sign of nervousness, the Senate Leadership Fund, the top super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, has now decided to spend $5 million on the race. In another, Trump unleashed an attack on Andrews, describing her three times in a Truth Social post with a slur for transgender people. (She is not transgender.) "Darline is a High Quality person, maybe the highest, and Annie Trannie is not," he wrote. His approval rating has softened in South Carolina, as elsewhere. On Oct. 6, the University of Virginia's Center for Politics moved its ranking of the race from "Safe Republican" to "Likely Republican." That is, still GOP-leaning. But no longer safe. How high could a blue tide rise? Watch: Kansas Senate, Marshall v. Hamilton The last time a Democratic candidate won a Senate race in Kansas, Babe Ruth was playing for the New York Yankees. And when Republican Roger Marshall was elected to the Senate six years ago, he swamped his Democratic opponent by double digits. Despite that friendly political terrain, Marshall was just three points ahead of Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton in a new You/Gov poll. Hamilton is the founder and senior pastor of the state's largest church, The Church of the Resurrection, in the Kansas City suburbs. In July, the Cook rankings categorized the race as "Solid Republican," then in August moved it to "Likely Republican," then in September moved it to "Lean Republican." On Oct. 6, the contest was moved to a "toss-up." At their first debate, Marshall blasted Hamilton as "too woke and too weak" for the Sunflower State. But he drew jeers and boos from the crowd who had packed the bleachers at the Kansas State Fair when he defended his loyalty to Trump. "Look, these tariffs are working," he insisted. "The current administration that Marshall supports is not normal," Hamilton replied. Susan Page, the Washington Bureau chief of USA TODAY (and a Kansas native), has covered the last 12 presidential elections. item.title: Christa Pike wasn't alone in her crime. What happened to the accomplices?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
While Christa Pike didn't act alone in the crime that landed her on death row , the two others involved in the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer met less severe punishments. Pike, Tadaryl Shipp and Shadolla Peterson were all students at Jobs Corps, a training program in Knoxville, Tennessee, when they lured Slemmer, a classmate, into the woods on Jan. 12, 1995. There, Pike and Shipp, a couple at the time, tortured Slemmer and bludgeoned her to death. They were both later convicted of the crime, while Peterson pled guilty and walked away with probation, according to court records. The grisly crime has garnered renewed interest after Pike's botched execution by lethal injection on Sept. 30. She was transported to a hospital and has since regained consciousness and is speaking , her attorney said on Oct. 7. Here's what to know about the other assailants in the case that's capturing national attention. Christa Pike accomplice Tadaryl Shipp serving life sentence Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit first-degree murder at a 1997 trial. He was sentenced to life and 25 years in prison, according to court and inmate records. Because Shipp was 17 at the time of the crime, he could not get the death penalty under state law. After Slemmer's murder, Shipp told police he "had dabbled in satanism since he was 10 years old," according to a 1998 appellate ruling. When he and Pike were taken into custody two days after the murder, they were both wearing pentagram necklaces, and Shipp told police he had "satanic paraphernalia" in his room at the Job Corps campus. Shipp told police he carved a pentagram into Slemmer's chest because he thought she could be "a satanic sacrifice." According to WATE and WBIR , Shipp was denied parole in October 2025. The 48-year-old will be eligible for parole again in 2031. Other accomplice, Shadolla Peterson, got probation Peterson, the other individual involved in the crime, pleaded guilty to being an accessory and received a sentence of six years probation, per court documents. She took a plea deal from prosecutors and received credit for 460 days in jail, according to a 1996 article in the Knoxville News Sentinel, part of the USA TODAY Network. While Peterson had initially been indicted on a murder charge, prosecutors said if the case had gone to trial, they would only have proof that she was present at the murder, not that she was involved in the killing, according to the article. The public defender who represented Peterson told the outlet at the time that she admitted to being present at the killing but denied taking part in the attack and did not know Slemmer was going to be murdered. What did Christa Pike do? On Jan. 12, 1995, Pike asked Slemmer to accompany her to a Blockbuster store before luring her into the woods, she told police. Pike – who had brought a box cutter and meat cleaver with her – and Shipp attacked Slemmer, bludgeoning her and eventually cutting her stomach and throat with the box cutter, according to court documents . During the attack, as Slemmer bargained for her life, Pike "told Slemmer to 'shut up' because it 'was harderto hurt somebody when they’re talking to you,'" she later told police, per court documents. Shipp also carved a pentagram into Slemmer's chest, and Pike – who told police she believed Slemmer was interested in her boyfriend – later showed off a piece of Slemmer's skull to a friend. Slemmer's body was found on Jan. 13, 1995. A Tennessee Grounds Department employee first mistook her body for the corpse of an animal because of how badly she had been beaten, according to court records . Born on Sept. 20, 1975, Slemmer was raised in Orange Park, Florida, but moved to Knoxville to enroll in Jobs Corps, according to court records and the Nashville Tennessean, part of the USA TODAY Network . More: Remembering Colleen Slemmer, the teenager killed by Christa Pike May Martinez, Slemmer's mother, told WBIR-TV that her daughter loved roller skating, computers and playing old games with her family. "She was a nerd," Martinez told the station. "But a good nerd." Christa Pike latest: Attorney says she is 'angry' after botched execution Officials in Tennessee attempted to execute Pike on Sept. 30, but she survived two doses of pentobarbital injections and was taken to a Nashville-area hospital. Pike's attorney Randy Spivey said she woke up and began speaking on Oct. 7. He believes the first words she said were, "where am I and who are you?" "She is angry and confused about everything right now," Spivey said, adding that she is "very aware the state tried to execute her." Pike has a blood clot in one of her arms, pneumonia and swelling in her hands and arms, Spivey said. She is unable to swallow or move her arms and it's unclear what kind of function she will regain. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has ordered an investigation into what went wrong and called off the state's only remaining lethal injection this year. Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada also announced his resignation after the incident. item.title: U.S. has lost or sustained damage to 81 aircraft worth up to $3.3 billion in Iran war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Airmen from the Texas Air National Guard conduct preflight and postflight inspections on an MQ-9 Reaper aircraft at Keflavík Air Base, Iceland, in August. - Senior Airman Edgar Grimaldo/US Air Force/File The United States military has had 81 aircraft destroyed or damaged in the war with Iran , a Congressional Research Service report released this week says. The number includes both airplanes and helicopters as well as drones, with the MQ-9 Reaper drone – used for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, close air support and combat search and rescue – accounting for more than half of the losses. But also on the list are some of the Pentagon’s most-prized assets, including an F-35A fighter jet and an E-3 Sentry , the four-engine jet with a large radar dome atop the fuselage used for target tracking and airspace management. The total cost of the aircraft lost is between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, depending on the Defense Department’s plans for replacements, the report said, citing figures from the Congressional Budget Office. The total cost of the war is much higher – at least $45 billion, sources have told CNN . That figure doesn’t include damage to infrastructure at US bases in the region, including those where some of the aircraft losses happened . Some of the aircraft included in the count may have been returned to service, including eight F-15 Strike Eagle fighter jets that sustained light damage in an Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan, in September. The report is based on numbers contained in statements from the Defense Department; its inspector general; US Central Command, which has been conducting the operations against Iran; and news reports reviewed by the CRS. The report poses several questions for congressional consideration, including whether lawmakers are getting enough information from the Pentagon on the losses to determine effects and remedies. Defense Department reporting on Iran war losses has , to date, been vague. Even the Pentagon inspector general’s report on the losses, released in September, and covering action from February 28 to June 30, cites previous CRS reports for some of its aircraft loss numbers. Other issues Congress needs to think about are whether to provide funding for repairs or replacements; whether there is enough industrial capacity to satisfy those requirements; and the effects on US military sales to foreign partners. It also raises questions about how the Iran war has affected US posture outside the Middle East. “Congress may assess whether losses in certain high-demand platforms that are aging and limited in number, such as the E-3 Sentry, create capability gaps or increase risk in other theaters,” the report says. item.title: Trump administration proposes $70,000 fee for international students to work in U.S.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Students walk through the University of Texas campus on Aug. 24, 2026. —Jay Janner—The Austin American-Statesman/Getty Images The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a rule that would charge schools $70,000 per international student seeking to work in the U.S. through a program known as Optional Practical Training. It marks the Trump Administration’s latest attempt to curb foreign enrollment . The proposal, published Thursday in the Federal Register and open for comment until Nov. 9, aims to crack down on OPT—a temporary employment authorization that lets students work in jobs related to their field of study and that DHS has claimed has “ballooned into an uncontrolled guest worker pipeline” and become a “magnet for fraud.” Under the current system, students pay about $500 to apply and are generally permitted to work in the U.S. for up to a year during or after their study, while those in the science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields may get work period extensions. Under the proposal, schools would have to pay $70,000 for a student’s initial participation—and another $30,000 for each additional program participation—though DHS said it recognizes schools “may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee” to students or employers. Collected fees would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury. A DHS spokesperson said in the announcement of the proposed fee that OPT “was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor, or a prize for those who game the system,” and that “American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been turned into a pipeline for cheap foreign labor.” International students have been in the crosshairs of the second Trump Administration as part of the President’s wider anti-immigration agenda. The Administration has revoked thousands of student visas and heightened vetting of applicants , including by reviewing their social media activity. It also pressured universities and colleges to agree to a compact that includes capping the number of undergraduate students on foreign visas , and it tried to limit the stays of international students to only four years. The Administration has zeroed in particularly on Chinese students amid national security concerns. While the Administration champions policies discouraging foreign student enrollment as a means to benefit Americans, experts have said that such policies could hamper U.S. competitiveness in the long run. Why DHS is cracking down on OPT Since 1947 , federal regulations have allowed foreign students to work in cases where employment for practical training is required or recommended by their schools. But DHS in May alleged it found more than 10,000 foreign students “who claim to be working for highly suspect employers,” and, upon further OPT-linked investigations across multiple states, said it found “empty buildings and locked doors at addresses where hundreds of foreign students are allegedly employed.” Investigators also alleged fraudulent activities, such as “phantom employees,” and suspicious financial transactions. In its proposal for the new fee, DHS claimed that the program’s growth in the last few years “has exponentially outpaced the number of companies” which it could review and investigate. It said that 194,554 students were granted employment authorization documents in 2024, compared to 160,627 in 2023. The department reasoned that “without the fees proposed in this rule, it cannot operate OPT consistent with its focus on preventing fraud and may shut down the program entirely.” It also said the fee was “necessary to ensure that schools, students, and employers participate in OPT for its intended purpose instead of a means to circumvent the H-1B visa program,” which refers to the work visa that allows American employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations such as technology, engineering, education, healthcare, and finance. OPT has often served as a bridge for students seeking work under H-1B visas, which the Administration has similarly targeted with higher fees . DHS said it believes that the proposed fee would put the onus on schools “to exercise greater oversight and selectivity” when recommending students for OPT, and it would thus reduce fraud. Critics call proposal illegal—and anti-American The proposal, however, like previous attempts to curb foreign enrollment, is expected to face legal challenges. On Oct. 5, educational organizations took the Administration to court following its efforts to limit a similar program, Curricular Practical Training. A $100,000 H-1B visa fee has also been blocked in courts . “Don’t Panic: DHS has no authority to slap a $70k fee on international students,” Doug Rand, director of the Talent Mobility Fund, an advocacy group for attracting foreign STEM talent, posted on LinkedIn . “Let’s not overreact—this proposed rule isn’t going to fare well in the courts, just as the $100k H-1B fee and other restrictionist policies have been struck down.” Todd Schulte, president of the immigration reform advocacy group FWD.us, said that if the proposal passes, the U.S. “is intentionally pricing itself out of the global market for top talent, especially in STEM fields.” Results of a survey by the D.C.-based think tank Institute for Progress released Tuesday found that most international students plan to use OPT, but 80% fewer students said “they would likely try to stay” if the proposed fees were implemented. For STEM students eligible for OPT, the survey found that only 15% would likely try to stay. “DHS assumes that for STEM grads, there will be ZERO change in participation,” the think tank’s director for immigration policy, Jeremy Neufeld, posted on X . Zuzana C. Wootson, deputy director of federal policy at nonprofit organization Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said in a statement that such exorbitant fees would push prospective students to competitor countries. But she also warned that the consequences “would extend well beyond international students. Declining international enrollment would strain institutional budgets, increase tuition pressure on American students, and diminish the educational experience for everyone.” This article originally appeared on Time at https://time.com/article/2026/10/08/international-student-training-opt-fee-work-trump-administration/

item.title: Democrats see a chance to flip deep-red states. But there's a catch.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats’ eyes may be bigger than their wallets. Democrats across a slate of deep-red states are clamoring for more cash to fight for Senate seats that suddenly seem within reach, with polling showing them competitive across a swath of normally impregnable territory from Kansas to Florida and South Carolina to Mississippi prompting a sudden bump in late-stage spending from outside groups. The party’s main campaign groups have already begun spending in Texas, another state they once downplayed that’s come seriously into play. But those same groups say they don’t have enough cash to protect the core battleground and also make significant investments beyond it — setting up Democrats for a series of difficult choices in the closing weeks of the midterms. “It’s very clear in the polling: If we get our message out, we're going to win. We're also not an expensive state to advertise in,” said Scott Colom, the Mississippi Democratic Senate nominee. “When it comes to Mississippi, we've been ignored for far too long.” Some Democrats see a generational opportunity to win seats in red states, driven by voters’ frustration with the economy that has hit rural and poorer red states particularly hard. And they’re starting to play around the edges. American Bridge PAC has pumped $2.1 million into Mississippi, where it is running ads targeting GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. The state’s population is poor and mostly rural — two groups that have been particularly squeezed by high gas prices. Democrats have long dreamed it could become competitive, and Hyde-Smith didn’t reach 55% of the vote in her two previous Senate wins. The PAC also on Wednesday put $2.5 million into Florida, $630,000 into South Carolina and over $410,000 into Kansas as part of a $22.7 million investment on 6,000 billboards focused on higher costs spanning roughly 80 House and Senate races, the group said. “We are very aware that a durable majority means we are going to have to compete in totally new places, in states where we haven’t competed before,” American Bridge 21st Century President Pat Dennis told POLITICO on Wednesday. “And we also know that those changes don’t happen all at once, they’re investments over years.” But Democrats, despite polling well, are being massively outspent on the airwaves across the core battleground states. They’re already heavily investing in a swath of states President Donald Trump won in 2024 by double-digit margins — Alaska, Iowa and Ohio and, most recently, Texas. And they’re wary of spending big in states where major money chasing good polls have yielded very little in past elections. “Across the board, this is belt-tightening time and campaigns and committees need to make sure the money is being spent on seats to secure a majority,” said one senior Democratic operative working on Senate races, granted anonymity to candidly discuss spending strategy. “The stark reality is there aren’t the funds at the national level to invest in the next ring of states without putting the genuine toss-ups at risk.” That comes after a new group affiliated with former Vice President Kamala Harris’ super PAC dropped nearly $700,000 into Kansas last week to benefit Democrat Adam Hamilton, on top of nearly $5 million in recent spending from an outside group backed by a local attorney. A group that backs Democratic doctors and scientists running for office, 314 Action, has bundled roughly $3.6 million for Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) recently transferred $250,000 toward Angie Nixon in Florida, an expensive former swing state. Those aren’t huge investments; Democrats have spent or reserved over $100 million in Ohio alone since Labor Day, according to data from tracking firm AdImpact. But Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has included both Kansas and Mississippi in his pitches to donors and hosted a fundraiser for Colom over the summer. He told reporters last week that “we’re going to do everything we can in as many states as we can.” Senate Majority PAC recently told POLITICO it is “actively thinking” about whether to wade into Kansas — even as the group, which posted a record third-quarter fundraising haul, warned last week in a memo to donors that “the resources we have now” are not enough to “expand into new opportunities.” Republicans are legitimately concerned about Kansas , where high diesel and fertilizer prices driven by the war with Iran are hitting farmers and ranchers hard — outside groups have poured in more than $10 million into the state in recent days. Public and private polls show Hamilton tied or in the lead . Danedri Herbert, the Kansas GOP chair, said she was confident Republican Sen. Roger Marshall will win reelection but is relieved national groups are now paying attention. “I wouldn't want to leave it to chance,” Herbert said. “We're glad they're here and taking it seriously.” In a statement, Hamilton spokesperson Tyson Brody said Washington Republicans are “panicking” and “sending in millions to try to distract from Marshall’s record.” Some Democrats see good reason to spend more in some of the smaller long-shot states. Their money can go a lot further in Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi — the same rationale they had when they invested in Alaska early this cycle but held off in Texas. "It's not a huge amount of money in these states. A little money goes a long way,” said Jaime Harrison, former Democratic National Committee chair and former Senate candidate in South Carolina. Democrats have been burned before by chasing these states. When Harrison ran for Senate in 2020, he raised $109 million . Polls showed a tight race before Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) beat him by 10 points. Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) told POLITICO late last month that “we should be adding Mississippi onto that roster.” “It’s also an issue of optimizing of money, right? Mississippi is a smaller market. So you might be able to invest and actually have great turnout,” Gallego said. Gallego also said he hopes to campaign with Nixon in Florida, who’s a “really good candidate” facing a “very expensive” media market. But most Democrats aren’t opening their wallets widely for Nixon, who joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June before her upset against well-funded establishment pick Alex Vindman in the primary. Nixon’s campaign has spent $64,000 on streaming ads so far, while Vindman spent $2 million on TV ads in the primary. Nixon met with Schumer last week and “had a really great conversation,” said her campaign manager, Eunic Epstein-Ortiz. She also said DSCC leadership has been “very supportive of the race.” Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), who chairs the campaign arm, held a virtual fundraiser for Nixon. In South Carolina, Andrews has posted healthy fundraising over a year into her campaign, which has helped her to blanket local broadcasts with ads for months against recently appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham. Polls have found a close race . Republicans are bearing down as well, putting $5 million for Graham in recent days. In a statement, a spokesperson for Andrews said the campaign has “the resources we need to share our message about lowering costs.” Kimberly Leonard and Lauren Fedor contributed to this report. item.title: Trump faces protests while rallying support for Paxton in Texas Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
SAN ANTONIO (AP) — President Donald Trump, facing protesters and a poor political climate, fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday night in a bid to stave off sweeping Democratic victories in the nation's most populous red state. But Trump's remarks were not focused solely on Paxton. Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump also pledged to award retired baseball star Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, restated his support for the death penalty for drug dealers and clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are “a small price to pay” for the war. “You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles,” Trump said. “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country.” The president's message was interrupted repeatedly by protesters, including by one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police. Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption. “He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.” Texas has become an unexpected battleground for Republicans The Republican Party did not plan to devote so much money and manpower to Texas this midterm season. Texas is the nation’s most populous reliably Republican state, where Trump won in 2024 by almost 14 percentage points. But with Election Day less than a month away, Trump’s poor approval ratings, the Iran war and soaring gas prices have threatened Republicans in virtually every state. Wednesday’s appearance marked Trump’s third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far. In a sign of Trump’s poor standing, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott did not attend the evening rally. A three-term Republican governor who won reelection in 2022 by roughly 11 percentage points, even Abbott has been caught in the turbulent national currents. He’s locked in a competitive reelection race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa . Instead of appearing with Trump, Abbott was scheduled to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on the governor’s absence. “For years, Greg Abbott has never been shy about embracing Donald Trump, calling Trump a ‘great friend’ and championing his agenda every step of the way,” said Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long. “But now, as Texas families get crushed by record-high prices driven by Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran, suddenly Greg Abbott has somewhere else to be.” Trump focuses on helping the Senate candidate he endorsed in GOP primary While the race for governor has drawn a sudden influx of cash from Democrats, the state’s U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention as Democrats fight for the chamber’s majority. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, but candidate James Talarico’s fundraising, Trump’s low approval rating and nagging concerns about Paxton’s character have put the race squarely in play. Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.” “He was tough and he was with us all the way,” Trump said of Paxton, whom he endorsed in the state's GOP primary over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. “He’s a fantastic man.” Trump made no mention of the recently leaked recording of Paxton lamenting the war in Iran and rising fuel prices, while also complaining his campaign was being run by operatives in Washington. He repeatedly criticized Talarico, including on the death penalty, a point that would appeal to many conservatives in the state that leads the nation in executions . Trump restated his support for the death penalty for “large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer,” while acknowledging that Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad. The president approved the method of execution earlier this week and suggested that Talarico opposes it. The Talarico campaign did not immediately respond when asked about the candidate’s position on Hasan’s scheduled execution. Paxton, invited onstage near the end of the rally, heaped praise on Trump, who stood behind him: “I am so grateful that you’re here." Trump makes a big announcement, but not about the Senate race While Trump promoted Paxton briefly at the beginning of his remarks, he spent almost as much time later talking up Clemens, the retired Red Sox and Yankees pitcher who has been denied a spot in Major League Baseball's Hall of Fame due to his alleged involvement with performance-enhancing drugs . Trump brought him onstage and said he'd be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, which is the highest civilian honor — and, Trump said, “a step up” from the Hall of Fame. Clemens said he was stunned by the honor. “This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” he said, standing alongside Trump. “And to get it from this man, this president. ... You talking about a winner? That’s a winner right there.” ___ Peoples reported from New York and Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press writer Will Weissert in Washington contributed. item.title: Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro and wife charged in U.S. over alleged torture
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Luc Cohen NEW YORK, Oct 8 (Reuters) - US prosecutors on Thursday charged ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores with conspiring to torture political opponents and American citizens, adding to the drug trafficking case the couple already faced. Separately, US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who is overseeing the case, denied a request ‌by Flores to be released from jail due to health concerns ahead of a trial scheduled for next year. Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, were captured on January 3 ‌in their Caracas home during a US military operation ordered by President Donald Trump, and were flown to New York to face drug charges against them that were announced that same day. A superseding indictment filed in Manhattan federal court ​on Thursday added the torture count to the existing criminal case. Maduro and Flores each would face a mandatory minimum 50 years in prison if convicted of all the charges. They have pleaded not guilty to the original charges, but have not yet entered pleas to the new indictment, which detailed alleged torture against nine people, including three US citizens. In a statement, Maduro's lawyer Barry Pollack said, "President Maduro denies the charges in the new indictment and looks forward to his day in court." Flores' lawyers Mark Donnelly and Andres Sanchez in a statement said their client denies the allegations. They questioned why prosecutors only revealed the ‌indictment, which court records showed was returned under seal by a grand ⁠jury on Tuesday, shortly before Thursday's hearing. "We look forward to fully responding to the allegations in court at the appropriate time," Donnelly and Sanchez said. Since Maduro's capture, Venezuela has boosted cooperation with the US under the leadership of his former Vice-President Delcy Rodriguez. Relations between the United States and oil-rich Venezuela were tense ⁠during the socialist Maduro's 13 years in power. US officials and human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but Thursday's indictment marked the first time Maduro faced criminal charges over the allegations. The indictment alleged that thousands of Venezuelans were threatened, arrested, tortured or killed at the hands of the state between 1999 and 2025. Before Maduro became president in 2013, both he and Flores held positions in the late Venezuelan ​President ​Hugo Chavez's government. 'A VIOLENT SYSTEM' "Maduro, Flores and other high-ranking members of their inner circle used a violent system ​of torture and repression to maintain their power," Jamie McDonald, the top ‌federal prosecutor in Manhattan, told reporters outside the courthouse after Flores' bail was denied. Flores was Venezuela's attorney general and led its National Assembly before becoming first lady. Many of the incidents of alleged torture described in the indictment occurred during times of political unrest in Venezuela or in response to perceived threats against Maduro. In one instance, prosecutors said, Maduro in 2013 ordered the arrest of a Venezuelan military officer he suspected of planning a coup. Members of Venezuela's military counterintelligence directorate then interrogated the officer while shocking the individual with a live electric wire around 20 times and hung the individual by the hands and feet for several minutes at a time, prosecutors said. In 2022, an American citizen detained while entering Venezuela was accused of conspiring to assassinate Maduro and was tortured by military ‌counterintelligence officers through beatings and shocks to the person's arms, legs and genitals, according to the indictment. FLORES DENIED ​RELEASE Flores' lawyers had argued their client should be released on bail because she needs a cardiac procedure and wants to ​recover in a more comfortable environment. The lawyers proposed moving her to a residence in ​the New York City area with round-the-clock private security, and said she is not a danger to the community. In denying the motion for bail, Hellerstein ‌decided the evidence against Flores appeared strong. The judge also said Flores, who ​wore a dark prison T-shirt and a headset ​to listen to a simultaneous Spanish translation of the proceedings, appeared to be relatively healthy. "For whatever it's worth, her appearance today is no worse and perhaps a little better than when I first met with her on her arraignment," Hellerstein said, referring to her first appearance in court on January 5. "She was still bandaged up from the military invasion," ​Donnelly said. Prosecutors in the Manhattan US Attorney's Office opposed Flores' release. They said ‌Flores has received adequate medical care at the detention center, and if released poses an "extreme" risk of flight and danger to the public, including possible witness intimidation. Hellerstein's bail ​denial will not affect Flores' trial or potential punishment. Maduro and Flores have been held at Brooklyn's Metropolitan Detention Center since their capture. Their trial is scheduled for ​June 1, 2027. (Reporting by Luc Cohen in New York; Editing by Bill Berkrot and Will Dunham) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/cilia-flores-wife-venezuelas-maduro-100347530.html

item.title: Cornell's Jane Doe is 'terrified' after police swatting incident, lawyer says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Cornell University campus on the night of October 6, 2026. Student leaders held a town hall to discuss fallout from the Jane Doe sexual assault case. - Surya Vaidy/CNN One month ago, the woman now known to America as Cornell’s Jane Doe was living in New York City among thousands of other aspirational twentysomethings, attempting to break into the hotel industry and build a new life, according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra. But that plan has been derailed since she filed a lawsuit against Cornell University and others, alleging she was raped at a frat house in 2024. Instead, Giuffra said, Doe spent Wednesday taping up paper to obscure the windows of her parents’ home out of fear that a gunman could attack her, and reeling from a swatting episode that he said prompted police to swarm their home Tuesday night with weapons drawn. Doe is increasingly scared for her own safety, Giuffra said in a phone interview with CNN on Wednesday as he detailed his client’s deteriorating mental state after an escalating series of violent threats. Officers pointed weapons at Jane Doe’s boyfriend, her brother and her father after receiving a bogus tip that “someone was killing people in the house” on Tuesday evening, he said. Death threats, doxxing attempts and an outpouring of anger online have also been levied at his client, Giuffra added. “I don’t think she’s in a good spot now,” Giuffra said. “She’s scared.” The public fallout from her allegations have rocked one of the country’s leading educational institutions. The university, its campus police force and the Tompkins County District Attorney’s office have each faced scrutiny over how they initially investigated her claims. Anger among students was palpable during a Wednesday sit-in on the Ithaca, New York, campus. Cornell students take part in a seven-hour sit-in protest on Wednesday. - Angelina Katsanis/Reuters Doe herself has been following media reports and social media posts on her case, Giuffra told CNN as he described a family reeling from a sudden and terrifying ordeal that punctured their sense of safety. “Before (this week), it was just a lunatic fringe, which you can be dismissive of,” he said. “Now it’s somebody taking real steps to harm you, and that’s pretty frightening.” Doe’s parents are furious after a fake tip to police, lawyer says At 7 p.m. on Tuesday evening, a police officer in Doe’s hometown was dispatched to respond to a disturbing call: A man had shot and killed his mother and then turned the gun on his sister. The information was bogus. But the officer, believing an active-shooter situation was unfolding, rushed to Doe’s home, where he saw a car backing out from the driveway, according to a police report from the incident obtained by CNN. As he apprehended the two men in the vehicle – later revealed to be Doe’s brother and her boyfriend – another figure emerged from the home’s doorway. “I’m the dad. What’s going on?” he yelled, according to the report. The man told police his daughter is Jane Doe of the Cornell case and that the family was “being threatened by numerous unknown people.” The swatting incident was an escalation in a series of threats to Doe’s safety that have roiled her family this week. The term “swatting” refers to false tips made to law enforcement agencies with the intention of having armed officers deployed to somebody’s home or place of business. “Luckily the brother was in his car, (he) put his hands up,” Giuffra told CNN on Wednesday, relaying the events of the night. “(Doe’s) boyfriend got thrown on the ground,” and her father also had “guns put in his face,” according to Giuffra. “If you had a trigger-happy cop, or somebody had done the wrong thing, somebody could have ended up dead,” he said. Police are now investigating the swatting attempt, and the FBI is also looking into the events, according to Giuffra. According to Doe’s lawyer and two police reports reviewed by CNN, police arrived moments after Doe received a separate phone call from somebody claiming to share a first name with one of the seven men she named in her civil complaint. According to her account to officers in the reports, Doe “began panicking” when she received the call, “because (her phone) wouldn’t stop ringing.” She informed officers about that previous call while they were at her house following the swatting tip. Before the night was over, Giuffra’s wife told him that she, too, had received a threatening phone call. “These people have done so much research into (Doe),” Giuffra said. It is not clear whether the separate threats cited in the police reports were connected. Giuffra said he was in contact with Doe and her family on Wednesday. Her parents are angry and she is terrified, he said. The lawyer shared with CNN an audio recording of a call he says was placed to his office on Wednesday afternoon. In the recording, a man identifies himself as “the person who called your client.” The man also is heard saying: “I’m telling you guys simply, I think you should advise your client to withdraw the case. Otherwise blood will be shed.” Doxxing attempts also have taken their toll Tuesday’s swatting attack was an escalation of the potential dangers facing Doe since she filed her lawsuit last month, but it was far from the only threat she’s received, her lawyer said. Giuffra estimated that dozens of threats have been made against her since mid-September, when his client filed a 101-page complaint alleging she had been sexually assaulted and raped by several members of the Xi chapter of Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity. The Chi Phi fraternity house on the campus of Cornell University. - Surya Vaidy/CNN Doe’s civil suit was filed against the university, the fraternity, seven fraternity members and others. It alleges that members of the frat drugged and sexually assaulted her in October 2024 and invited other fraternity members in a group chat to join the assault. The suit also alleges the school failed to protect her and adequately punish the accused students, who all deny wrongdoing. Giuffra detailed to CNN another threat: a text message, sent to Doe’s phone on Monday, with three emojis depicting guns. Meanwhile, a handful of online personalities with large followings have led a campaign to uncover the identity of Doe, whose name was redacted in legal documents. One wrote on X to 347,000 followers in late September: “If you happen to know who this Cornell ‘Jane Doe’ is, get in touch and I would be happy to publish her name and identifying information.” He later claimed to have identified her and said he shared that identity online before deleting his post. Such behavior is known as doxxing, or sharing someone’s personal information or identity online without their permission. It has left Doe frightened and struggling to come to terms with the impact of the lawsuit, which has prompted outrage and scrutiny of how the university and its private police force initially investigated her claims. On Wednesday, Doe was “taping paper over windows in the house she’s lived at her whole life,” Giuffra said, “so people can’t see into her house to take a shot at her.” “I don’t get shook up very easily, but this shook me up. I didn’t want to have a body on my hands,” he said. “The dad is … concerned for his daughter. He can’t believe this has happened out of something where she’s just trying to stand up for herself and be heard,” Giuffra added. “But the parents are really strong people, and they’re going to protect their daughter.” Her career dream is ‘lost’ Doe had studied hotel administration at Cornell’s prestigious Nolan School of Hotel Administration, and it had been her “dream” to attend the school, Giuffra said. Her complaint says she traveled across the country and arrived at the school with the same “hopes, expectations and trepidations of other high school graduates.” But she left the program without graduating after the alleged assault took place two years ago. item.title: Long-deployed USS Abraham Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
CORONADO, Calif. (AP) — Sailors began disembarking the USS Lincoln on Thursday following a deployment that included a record 265 uninterrupted days at sea and reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew. Families waiting for the aircraft carrier’s arrival in San Diego Bay described crying and losing sleep after hearing about the ship’s food shortages and tough conditions. Many said the sailors had sent lists of the food they were craving. Dozens of sailors stood atop the carrier as it glided past the cityscape of downtown San Diego toward cheering families who were carrying flowers and balloons and ringing cowbells. Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck. "It feels really overwhelming,” she said about being reunited, adding she's glad her mom won't need to eat ramen almost every day. The carrier drew national attention following reports of stress among the crew and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products, during its Iran war mission. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation , the highest honor a unit can receive. Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the “Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission.” USS Lincoln crew looks forward to family and favorite meals Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado will be 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said. Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her six-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress. “She’s our deployment baby,” said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia. “We are different people now; we are parents now,” she said. “We definitely matured from the last time we saw each other.” It was tough to hear about the ship’s conditions while she was pregnant, she said. “I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn’t sure if he was OK or not,” she said. When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was “pretty bad.” Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas to name a few. He had told his wife about “the lack of food and showers” on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned 4 while he was away, she said. The Navy initially downplayed problems on the carrier The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment was “not nearly long enough.” Hegseth told the crew that “what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you’re resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless.” The carrier left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28. Navy leaders eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard. In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced for a short time. After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln’s crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East. Long deployments can tax service members Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment. The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months. According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed nearly 3,700 combat missions, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, and destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles. The Lincoln, which set a record for days between ports of call, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment during the Iran war and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward, typically reserved for significant achievement in combat. The crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford returned in May from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The deployment didn’t include as many uninterrupted days at sea as the Lincoln. Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington , relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August. ___ Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. item.title: Newly obtained footage shows Iran attack on major U.S. post in Kuwait early-on in war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — New videos obtained exclusively by CBS News show Iranian attacks on a major U.S. military base in Kuwait as the war with Iran kicked off seven months ago. American forces faced ballistic missiles, drones and what witnesses described as Iranian F-5 fighter jets. The footage obtained by CBS News was recorded by a person stationed on the ground at Camp Buehring, and captures the moments of impact and their explosive aftermath. Damage to buildings and military equipment can also be seen in the videos. The attacks on Camp Buehring offer a window into the strain Iranian attacks placed on American forces during the opening days of the war. CBS News has learned that soldiers defending the base ran critically low on .50-caliber ammunition as some soldiers were repositioned into the Udari Desert in Kuwait. Two soldiers were injured by lightning there in late April, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter. Contacted by CBS News, U.S. Central Command, the primary unit which oversees American military operations across the Middle East, declined to comment. The Pentagon did not comment, but pointed back to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments on March 4 regarding the removal of U.S. troops from bases and the employment of defensive measures. "As we built up offensive combat power, we moved the vast majority of American troops — over 90% of Americans that were on our bases — what we say off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire," Hegseth told reporters in March. Camp Buehring, or CBKU, sits about 25 miles from the Iraqi border and has for more than two decades served as a major staging ground for American forces deploying across the Middle East. CBS News authenticated the videos using metadata embedded in the files and compared the footage to other photographs showing damage to the base. Ahead of the war, sources said most of the roughly 7,000 troops there were moved elsewhere — as were the majority of U.S. forces in Kuwait — as a part of the Pentagon's "get off the X" plan, military shorthand for moving away from a position vulnerable to attack. Once the war started, Iranian attacks, some originating from Iraq, repeatedly threatened the installation. Missiles and drones forced soldiers into bunkers. Three U.S. service members told CBS News that Iranian F-5 fighter jets were also used during the attacks, a detail first reported in April by NBC News. "They ran so close to us I could see their helmets," the eyewitness described. "They came in, they hit us, and then took off." While most of the U.S. service members were moved off of Camp Buehring, a tranche of more than 100 soldiers stayed behind. The service members feared the isolated base was ill-equipped to handle a mass-casualty event if the attacks continued. "They hit us bad," the source told CBS News on condition of anonymity because of the military's strict media restrictions. "It was horrible. There were a lot of brave guys who stayed to fight there — and people at home don't know what happened. We had to abandon the base." A senior Army official working in logistics, managing operations from another post in Kuwait, confirmed to CBS News there were concerns about the availability of .50 caliber ammunition and other "exquisite" munitions like Patriot missile batteries. The decision ultimately was to leave. Service members packed up, loading their vehicles with whatever equipment they could and drove at night deep into the Kuwaiti desert. Their remote locations would emerge as forward operating bases, or "FOBs," where the soldiers would remain indefinitely. No one was killed by enemy fire at Camp Buehring or at the FOBs, but several were injured, including two soldiers who were struck by lightning in desert sandstorms. One soldier suffered burns after the direct strike while the other suffered a ruptured eardrum, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter. Before the lightning strike, Army leaders had been trying to move the troops out of the area, but were not able to do so quickly enough. In May, the soldiers left the FOBs for Camp Arifjan, and then relocated to other positions both in and out of the Middle East. "CBKU got demolished," the source added. "They need to do an investigation. How come no one came to reinforce us?" The Defense Department's inspector general last month released a report on the war with Iran that revealed "equipment losses" worth up to $3.7 billion — including nearly 60 aircraft. On Monday, the Congressional Research Service, which provides nonpartisan analysis to members of Congress, reported that 81 fixed or rotary-wing aircraft including drone assets had been lost or damaged by Iran since February, according to news reports and statements from the Defense Department. In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector general added that U.S. Central Command had reported Iranian strikes at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. Although strikes were mentioned in the report, pictures and videos of any impact zones have been extremely limited. Beyond Camp Buehring, CBS News earlier obtained exclusive photos of damage at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait. CBS News has also reported extensively on the deadliest attack of the war against U.S. troops at the Port of Shuaiba, which killed six American service members.
